analysis.one_liner: Creates a government-run health insurance plan to compete with private insurers on the new health exchanges.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on July 21, 2010, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have added a public health insurance option to the Affordable Care Act: a plan run by the federal government and sold through the new health insurance exchanges alongside private plans. It would have to follow the same coverage rules as private plans, charge premiums set to cover its own costs, and pay doctors and hospitals at rates tied to Medicare's, which are typically lower than what private insurers pay. The aim was to give people buying coverage a cheaper choice and to pressure private insurers to lower prices. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it died in the Energy and Commerce Committee when the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance through the exchanges would gain a government-run plan option that must follow the same rules as private plans but pays providers at Medicare-based rates, which are lower, making it likely to offer cheaper premiums. Small businesses buying on the exchanges would benefit too, and the bill also requires the plan to work to reduce racial and ethnic health disparities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People buying their own health coverage

how_it_helps.text: Creates a federally run health plan sold alongside private plans on the Exchanges, with the Secretary required to design it as a low-cost option that preserves quality and access.
The plan must offer bronze, silver, and gold coverage tiers and follow the same consumer protections, benefits, and cost-sharing rules as private Exchange plans.

Its payment rates start from Medicare rates, which are generally lower than what private insurers pay, and the Secretary may use delivery reforms like bundled payments and medical homes to hold costs down.
Enrollees get Medicare-style access to federal courts to enforce their rights, and an ombudsman office handles complaints.

analysis.who_pays: Private health insurers would face a new, lower-priced competitor on the exchanges, and doctors and hospitals would be paid at Medicare-based rates rather than higher private rates for patients enrolled in the plan. Taxpayers front $2 billion in start-up funding plus 90 days of claims reserves, but the bill requires that money to be repaid within ten years.

drawbacks.text: The public option had to be self-financing from premiums alone, with start-up funds of $2 billion plus 90 days of claims reserves repaid to the Treasury over ten years, giving it no public subsidy to undercut private insurers on price.

To build a doctor network it had to offer providers payment rates 5 percent above Medicare rates for the first three years and let providers opt out, which limited its ability to drive prices down below private insurers' costs.
The plan was available only inside the Exchanges, so people with employer coverage or Medicare would not benefit from it directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main drawback an honest supporter would acknowledge: the option had to pay its own way, with no sustained public subsidy, and offered hospitals and doctors only a temporary 5 percent incentive to participate, so the promise of lower premiums depended on an untested insurer competing on a supposedly level playing field. Even sympathetic analysts questioned whether it could hold down costs. Against that, the bill would have cost taxpayers little — the $2 billion start-up loan and 90 days of claims reserves had to be repaid within ten years — and would have given working families buying coverage on their own a cheaper, more accountable choice alongside private plans. It died without a hearing or vote, so its design was never tested in the open.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 21, 2010 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce — the only action it ever received.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever took place, and the bill expired with the 111th Congress in January 2011.
129 House Democrats cosponsored the bill, but the majority leadership did not bring it to the floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers are better off, since the government-run competitor they opposed never came to a vote and their role on the Exchanges was never threatened.

for.name: 129 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including senior members like Clyburn, Waxman, and George Miller.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor or scheduled it for committee action after the public option failed during the 2010 ACA negotiations.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Ran a sustained lobbying and advertising campaign against a public option during the ACA debate, the same policy this bill would revive.

sides.party_line_note: All 129 cosponsors were House Democrats, roughly half the Democratic caucus; no Republican supported it, and the all-Democratic coalition was not enough to get the bill a hearing.

industries.note: The bill would have put a government-run plan in direct competition with private insurers on the Exchanges, competing on price with the backing of Medicare-scale payment rates. Insurers, which lobbied hard against a public option during the ACA debate, would have faced the strongest pressure to lower premiums. [S2, S3] — note: the ACA lobby record is general knowledge context; the bill's competitive effect is from the sources.

Providers would gain up to 5 percent above Medicare rates for three years and automatic participation unless they opt out, but the plan's mandate to keep per-enrollee costs down and its Medicare-based rates would press on reimbursement over time. [S3]

Drugs not covered under Medicare would be priced at rates negotiated directly by the Secretary, a stronger negotiating position than private plans or (at the time) Medicare itself, threatening higher drug prices. [S3]
